_comment: Config for tool_temperature_graph.py -- a read-only visualization, no
settings here can change the g-code itself, only how the graph renders.
The M104 warmup/cooldown ramp durations themselves are NOT configured
here -- they come from tool_preheat.json's target_lead_seconds/
disable_unused_tool_temps.py, so the graph can't drift out of sync with
the actual ramp assumptions those two processors are using. See
tool_preheat.json for those two settings. M109 (wait-for-temp) ramps
are the one exception -- see m109_settle_seconds below, which IS local
to this file, since it's a pure rendering choice with no bearing on
actual g-code timing the way the other two are.
_tool_colors: Comma-separated hex colors, one per tool in tool order (position 0 = T0's color, position 1 = T1's, etc). Add or remove entries freely -- there's no fixed tool count here, it's auto-detected from the g-code. Leave blank (the default) to use each tool's ACTUAL filament color as loaded in the slicer for this export instead, read straight from the g-code's own filament_colour -- only falls back further to an auto-generated color, spread across the hue wheel, for a tool neither of those has anything for. Any entry you DO set here always wins outright over both fallbacks, for that tool.
_curve_style: 'line' draws each tool's curve as a colored line only. 'area' fills the area under each tool's curve (translucent, so overlapping tools are still visible underneath each other). 'area_line' draws both -- the filled area plus a solid line on top for definition.
_line_width_px: Width, in pixels, of the line itself (used by 'line' and 'area_line'). No effect on 'area' alone.
_area_alpha: Opacity (0-1) of the filled area under each tool's curve (used by 'area' and 'area_line'). Real translucency on the printer/browser-rendered side; approximated with a dither pattern in OrcaStrator's own Tk progress window, since classic Tk has no true alpha compositing. Lower it if several tools' filled areas overlapping gets visually noisy; 1.0 makes it fully opaque (later-drawn tools will occlude earlier ones wherever they overlap).
_m109_settle_seconds: How long (seconds) an M109 (wait-for-temp) command's ramp takes to draw, warming or cooling alike. M109 BLOCKS the print until its target is genuinely reached -- unlike fire-and-forget M104, there's no 'did it get there before something else interrupted it' question to model, so it doesn't use target_lead_seconds/target_cooldown_seconds from tool_preheat.json the way M104 does. Pure rendering choice local to this graph (not shared with insert_missing_tool_preheat.py/disable_unused_tool_temps.py, since it has no bearing on actual g-code timing) -- lower it toward 0 for a near-vertical jump, raise it if a short settle ramp reads as too abrupt at your canvas size.
_reference_lines_enabled: Draws a full-width horizontal line at every distinct temperature actually commanded somewhere in the g-code (0 excluded, since that's 'off' rather than a temperature) -- e.g. lines at 250 and 170 if those are the only two S-values used anywhere. Makes it easy to see at a glance whether a tool's curve actually reached a temp it was supposed to. In 'stacked' layout, the same set of lines repeats in every lane at the same relative height, not just the lanes where that particular tool used that particular temp.
_reference_line_color: Hex color of the reference lines. Independent of every tool's own curve color, since a reference line isn't tied to any one tool -- it's a shared value across all of them.
_reference_line_opacity: Opacity (0-1) of the reference lines. Kept well under 1.0 by default so they read as a background guide rather than competing with the tool curves themselves for attention.
_reference_line_style: 'dashed', 'dotted', or 'solid'. Dashed/dotted keep a reference line visually distinct from the tool curves crossing it (which are always solid); solid draws an unbroken line instead.
_reference_line_labels_enabled: Prints the temperature value (e.g. '250C') just above each reference line, so it's readable at a glance without having to match a line's height against the temperature axis by eye.
_reference_line_label_size_px: Roughly how large a label reads at this processor's own default ~500px-wide canvas -- unlike reference_line_width_px above, this ISN'T a literal final pixel size: a label scales up or down together with the rest of the graph (bigger canvas, bigger label) rather than staying fixed regardless of how large the graph itself ends up, so it stays legible and correctly proportioned at any canvas size.
_tool_labels_enabled: Identifies which curve belongs to which tool. In 'stacked' layout, each lane gets a small, colored 'T<n>' label in its own top-right corner (opposite the reference lines' own temp label), with extra headroom reserved above each lane so the label stays clear of a curve holding at peak temp. In 'overlay' layout -- where every tool shares the same band, so a corner label wouldn't say which curve is which -- this instead draws a centered legend below the graph: each tool's 'T<n>', colored to match its curve. Only shown in overlay mode with more than one tool on screen.
_tool_label_size_px: Same approximation as reference_line_label_size_px above (scales WITH the graph's canvas rather than staying a literal fixed pixel size). In overlay mode this also sets how much extra vertical room gets reserved below the plot for the legend, so a larger label size means a taller legend band too, not just bigger text.
_y_max_celsius: Auto/override for the top of the temperature axis. Leave null (Auto) to use the highest commanded target temp across every tool in this file, plus a small margin. Set a fixed number instead to keep the scale consistent when comparing graphs across different prints.
_tool_change_time_seconds: How many seconds a single toolchange's swap/purge/park routine costs, added to the timeline once per toolchange that's already happened by a given point -- the underlying time estimate treats a toolchange line itself as instantaneous, so without this every event's position runs early. Leave null (Auto) to read OrcaSlicer's own '; machine_tool_change_time = N' line from the file (falls back to 0 if that line isn't present). Set a fixed number to override it.
_print_duration_seconds: Sets the timeline's right edge -- the naive time model otherwise only ever reaches the LAST temperature-setting command's own timestamp, so any stretch of the print after that (nothing left to heat/cool, still printing) would be silently missing from the graph. Leave null (Auto) to read OrcaSlicer's own '; estimated printing time (normal mode) = XhYmZs' line from the file. Only ever extends the axis, never shrinks it below the last event's own time. Set a fixed number to override it.
_min_tools: Skip rendering entirely if fewer than this many tools have any temperature-setting command in the file -- nothing meaningful to graph with 0.
_svg_target: Where the graph shows up: 'pc' = only in OrcaStrator's own progress window at export time. 'printer' = only embedded in the g-code for the printer's own console/screen to render (via the same _SVG_TOOLS Klipper macro every other processor's SVG output uses). 'both' = show it in both places. No 'off' option -- this whole processor exists to show this, so hiding it everywhere isn't a meaningful choice.
_canvas_width_px: Width, in pixels, of the rendered graph. Independent of canvas_height_px below -- each is solved for directly, not derived from the other via a fixed aspect ratio.
_canvas_height_px: Height, in pixels, of the rendered graph. Independent of canvas_width_px above.
_layout: 'overlay' draws every tool's curve on the same 0..axis-max band, so overlapping tools sit on top of each other -- curve_style/area_alpha above exist mainly to keep that readable. 'stacked' instead gives each tool its own horizontal lane, offset vertically so nothing ever overlaps -- same temperature scale in every lane (not a separate scale per tool), just shifted, so relative peaks stay directly comparable by height. Lanes run top-to-bottom in tool order (T0 on top). Falls back to 'overlay' automatically when the file only has one tool -- stacking a single lane buys nothing.
_stack_lane_height_px: Height, in pixels, of each tool's own lane -- used only when layout is 'stacked'. The graph's total rendered height becomes (this x tool count) + (stack_gap_px x (tool count - 1)), OVERRIDING canvas_height_px above rather than being constrained by it, so stacking more tools makes the graph taller instead of squeezing existing lanes smaller.
_stack_gap_px: Vertical gap, in pixels, between adjacent lanes -- used only when layout is 'stacked'.
_debug: Writes a structured JSON snapshot of every tool's computed curve -- its segments, the events that produced them, and the resolved axis extents -- to a file. Exists so a 'why did this render the way it did' question can be answered from exact real data instead of a screenshot or a description of one, and is also what the Settings GUI's live preview renders against (see gui/tool_temperature_graph.py). Written on every run, including a skipped one. See helpers/debug_dump.py, the feature shared across every processor that opts in. Saved as tool_temperature_graph_debug.json.

debug._enabled: On by default. The file gets overwritten every run, so it always just reflects the latest gcode processed -- fine to leave on.

_notice: Whether this processor's own info/warning NOTICE messages show up on the printer console (via ORCASTRATOR_RENDER). The notice is still always written into the g-code's ORCASTRATOR_LOG block either way -- this setting only tells the printer-side macro whether to actually print it, so nothing is lost from the file or from this processor's own debug dump if debug logging is on, just muted on the console. abort-level notices (a genuine refuse-to-print condition, if this processor ever emits one) are NEVER muted by this, regardless of the setting -- see helpers/notice.py. Handy for decluttering the console around a gcode_template_notice.py template you actually want to stand out.

notice._display: Whether this processor's own info/warning NOTICE messages show up on the printer console (via ORCASTRATOR_RENDER). The notice is still always written into the g-code either way -- this only tells the printer-side macro whether to print it, so nothing is lost from the file or from a Debug dump if that's on, just muted on the console. Handy for decluttering the console around a gcode_template_notice.py template you actually want to stand out. A genuine abort/refuse-to-print notice, if this processor ever emits one, is never muted by this setting.
